title: Retained hidden excess generates memory in price-limited markets
abstract: The daily return of a stock is often restricted to an exchange-imposed band to curb extreme fluctuations. Any attempted price movement beyond this band is clipped, leaving an unobserved excess. We introduce a minimal stochastic latent-state model in which a fraction of this hidden excess is retained for the next day. This retention generates memory, even though the daily stochastic driving shocks are independent. For symmetric driving shocks with regularly varying tails, the stationary latent return preserves the tail index of the noise, but has an enhanced tail amplitude. In the wide-band limit, a close of the daily return at either limit of the band admits a single-dominant-shock description. We show that after such an event, the mean return on the following day has the same sign and grows proportionally to the band width, while the probability of reaching the same limit again approaches a finite value. Reaching the opposite band limit on the following day requires a second extreme shock of opposite sign and is power-law suppressed. Simulations support these analytical predictions. Empirical data from stocks subject to daily price limits are qualitatively consistent with the predicted same-sign response and its increase across wider price bands.
summary: This paper models financial returns subject to exchange price limits, treating the resulting 'hidden excess' as a latent variable that carries over time. By analyzing this memory mechanism using stochastic processes, it predicts how limit hits influence subsequent market behavior, showing persistent directional bias proportional to the band width.
main_problem: The study investigates how an unobserved 'hidden excess' generated by clipping extreme fluctuations (price limits) in financial markets generates memory in subsequent price movements, even when the underlying driving shocks are independent.
main_result: In the wide-band limit, a limit close leads to a next-day mean return of the same sign that grows proportionally to the band width, and the probability of hitting the same limit again approaches a finite value.
method: The analysis employs a minimal stochastic latent-state model, deriving analytical results for stationary dynamics and performing asymptotic analyses in the wide-band limit.
model_or_system: The system models daily stock returns constrained by exchange-imposed symmetric price bands $[-C, C]$. The memory is introduced via a retention mechanism where a fraction of the unobserved excess from clipping is carried forward to influence the next day's latent return.
key_observables: Next-day mean return sign/magnitude, persistence probability (same limit hit), and reversal probability (opposite limit hit).
important_parameters:
Band width ($C$), retention coefficient ($\lambda$), and the tail index ($
u$) of the driving shocks.
main_assumptions: The model assumes a latent-state process where the hidden excess is retained, and it utilizes the single-dominant-shock description in the wide-band limit.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate information loss at limit closes (Fig 1), the renormalization of the stationary latent density amplitude due to retention (Fig 2), and representative trajectories showing persistent excess leading to consecutive limit closes (Fig 3).
paper_structure: The paper develops a stochastic latent-state model for price-limited returns, analyzes its stationary dynamics under heavy tails, derives asymptotic results in the wide-band limit, and validates these predictions using simulations and empirical data from global indices.
why_interesting: While applied to finance, the core mathematical structure—modeling memory generation via unobserved state variables constrained by boundaries—is analogous to studying non-equilibrium dynamics or boundary effects in physical systems like charge transport or particle confinement.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Possible intraday evolution of the running return rt(τ) under a symmetric return band with limits at ±C. The realized daily return is the closing value Rt = rt(τclose). A limit close records Rt = ±C but does not reveal the magni- tude of the underlying excess demand or supply. Note that the discrete-time quantity Rt does not resolve the intermedi- ate intraday path; the model instead maps the state directly from one market close to the next.

FIG. 2. Positive-tail collapse of the stationary latent den- sity p(x) confirming the amplitude renormalization (6) with C = 0.1 and ν = 3.5. Symbols are obtained from stationary trajectories of length 1010 generated by numerical simulations using Student’s t driving shocks with degrees of freedom ν and scale parameter sϵ = 0.01 [see Appendix B].

FIG. 3. Representative discrete-time trajectory of the latent return Xt, realized return Rt, and hidden excess Lt = Xt−Rt. The large negative shock at t1 produces a short-lived lower- limit close, whereas the large positive shock at t2 generates a persistent hidden excess and consecutive upper-limit closes. Horizontal dotted lines mark the return limits ±C, vertical dashed lines mark the shock times, and connecting lines are guides to the eye.

FIG. 4. (a) Post-upper-limit-close response m+ as a function of the return-limit magnitude C for λ = 0.5; dashed lines denote the analytical result (28). Symbols are obtained from stationary trajectories of length 1010 generated by numerical simulations using Student’s t driving shocks with degrees of freedom ν and scale parameter sϵ = 0.01 [see Appendix B]. (b) Limiting normalized response m+/C in the (λ, ν) plane obtained from Eq. (28).

FIG. 5. (a) Same-limit persistence probability P++(C) and (b) opposite-limit reversal probability P+−(C) as functions of the return-limit magnitude C for ν = 3.5. Symbols are ob- tained from stationary trajectories of length 1010 generated by numerical simulations using Student’s t driving shocks with ν degrees of freedom and scale parameter sϵ = 0.01 [see Ap- pendix B]. The horizontal dashed lines in (a) show the wide- band limit in Eq. (32), while the dashed line in (b) shows the C−ν decay predicted by Eq. (33).
